sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source belongs to the Schio-Vicenza fault system, a NW-SE trending, NE-dipping, set of high angle faults that lower the sedimentary succession of the Veneto plain to the east (e.g. Pola et al., 2014), being a transverse structure with respect to the general trend of the Eastern Southern Alps thrust front. The main structure of this fault system is the Schio-Vicenza Line, a NW-SE, 120 km long, steep strike-slip fault (e.g. Pellegrini, 1988; Castaldini and Panizza, 1991; Zampieri et al., 2003, 2021). The Schio-Vicenza Line is a prominent geomorphological lineament across the Southern Alps and the Venetian Po Plain, bordering to the east the Lessini, Berici and Euganei Mts., fragments of the Alpine retro-foreland (Bigi et al., 1992). To the south-east, this prominent lineament continues in the subsurface of the Veneto plain, where it is known as the Conselve-Pomposa fault (Pola et al., 2014).
The Schio-Vicenza fault system has undergone different tectonic phases of activity, showing different kinematics at least since the Mesozoic to the Quaternary (see Zampieri et al., 2021). Nowadays, the Schio-Vicenza Line is an inherited and well-developed structural element with a significant imprint in the landscape, reactivated in the current stress regime. The analysis of the longitudinal profiles of the fluvial terraces close to Schio shows Pleistocene differential uplift across the fault system, with the western block (footwall) of the Schio-Vicenza Line uplifted with respect to the plain (Pellegrini, 1988). On the other hands, at Isola Vicentina, ca. 10 km southeast of Schio, Miocene sediments dip 50Â° towards northeast, representing the limb of a drag fold of the footwall. If the long-term dip-slip component of faulting is well defined, on the contrary the horizontal component is not as well constrained.
Unfortunately, apart from moderate seismicity near its northern end (e.g. ViganÃ² et al., 2008) and the geological evidence of recent deformation of a travertine mound close to the Euganei Mts. (Pola et al., 2014), as a whole there is little evidence to constrain the recent activity of Schio-Vicenza Line, and even its role in the geodynamic framework of the Southern Alps is still a matter of debate. Although its kinematics is still largely unknown, we observe that it interrupts the continuity of the Southern Alps thrust front in the Veneto sector (Thiene-Cornuda thrust), suggesting that it played a passive role in controlling the geometry of the active fault systems and the current distribution of seismic moment release.
As a matter of fact, the true kinematics of this fault system is ambiguous, since along its portion northwest of the Thiene-Bassano thrust front earthquake focal mechanisms have dextral strike-slip kinematics on the NW-SE trending focal planes. Conversely, few kinematic indicators found along its south-eastern portion, along with geological features, suggest sinistral movements. Geodynamic considerations suggest a role of the Schio-Vicenza fault system similar to that of the Dinaric system, being presently characterized by dextral strike-slip kinematics (like the Predijama, Idrija and Ravne faults), and accommodating to the east the indentation of Adria against the Alpine chain (e.g. Moulin et al., 2016). If that is the case, the Schio-Vicenza system should have a sinistral component of motion, having the same orientation of the Dinaric system, yet bordering the Venetian foredeep to the west. However, instrumental seismicity data in the northern part of the Schio-Vicenza Line indicate a dextral strike-slip activity, which is also corroborated by field analysis of a N-S Riedel of the fault cropping out in its north-western part, just north of the Borcola Pass (Fondriest et al., 2012). While further evidence on the kinematics of the Schio-Vicenza line shall arise solely from the results of further research in the area, the apparently conflicting data and considerations can be reconciled in the sinistral opening "zipper" model (Platt and Passchier, 2016; Passchier and Platt, 2017), where intersecting pairs of simultaneously active faults with different sense of shear merge into a single fault. If this the case, the junction of the three branches would be located at PÃ²sina, ca. 10 km northwest of Schio, where the Schio-Vicenza and the Gamonda fault merge (Zampieri et al., 2003; Zampieri and Massironi, 2007). In this model, the Schio-Vicenza fault kinematics would be dextral in the sector north of PÃ²sina, and sinistral south of PÃ²sina, respectively (Zampieri et al., 2021).
In spite of the lack of historical and instrumental seismological evidence, we suggest that the Schio-Vicenza Line may host significant earthquakes. As a matter of fact, it does not appear to have generated earthquakes equal or larger than magnitude 5.0. Historical and instrumental catalogues (e.g. Rovida et al., 2021) show only a scattered distribution of moderate seismicity along this structure. Moreover, the source of the 13 September 1989, Mw 4.9 earthquake, having a depth of 40 km and a dextral strike-slip kinematics (Pondrelli et al., 2006), is located north of Schio and falls within the Schio-Vicenza fault system, and is thus deemed responsible for the 1989 event (Vannoli et al., 2015). Other instrumental earthquakes occurred near the northern part of the structure and showed dextral strike-slip focal mechanisms (ViganÃ² et al., 2008; ViganÃ² et al., 2015). Among these, the 16 June 2000, Mw 3.7 earthquake occurred near Rovereto along the northernmost sector of this fault system (Braunmiller et al., 2002).
The length of this Source is constrained by structural, seismological, and geomorphological data for the northwestern sector (Pellegrini, 1988; Fondriest et al., 2012), and by seismic and subsurface geological data for the southeastern one (Finetti, 1972; Pola et al., 2014). The strike of this Source was based on that of the mapped structure. The dip was based on geological data and seismic profiles data. As for the rake, we chose the right-lateral strike-slip solution on the basis of geological and seismological data collected in the northern sector of the fault system, and also of its strike and the relative orientation with respect to the stress field. The minimum and maximum depth were based on subsurface geological and geophysical data. The slip rate was inferred from geodynamic data and geological considerations.

pictures.c: Cross-sections  sub-orthogonal to the Schio-Vicenza Line obtained through the interpretation of the seismic sections. Fault traces associated with the Schio-Vicenza Fault System are recognized. SV: Schio-Vicenza fault; CP: Conselve-Pomposa fault; TC: Travettore-Codevigo fault; M: Mesozoic extensional fault; A: Apennine reverse fault (from Pola et al. [2014]).

Map of the depth of the Pliocene base along the Schio-Vicenza Fault System (SVFS), Travettore-Codevigo fault (TC) and Conselve-Pomposa fault (CP). Notice the deepening toward southeast due to the Apennine Pliocene-Quaternary flexuring. IFS: Idrija Fault System (from Pola et al. [2014]).

Tensional fracture on the Upper Pleistocene travertine mound in Abano Terme, southwest of Padova. This fracture has been referred to a releasing stepover of the Schio-Vicenza buried faults (from Pola et al. [2014]).

Mesozoic structural domain in the southern Alps. The Mesozoic extension resulted in the creation of a northsouth half graben, bounded by east- and west-dipping master normal faults. Four paleogeographical-structural units are recognizable; from west to east: (1) the Lombardian Basin; (2) the Trento platform and plateau; (3) the Belluno Basin; and (4) the Friuli platform (Masetti et al., [2012])
